item.title: Introduction
item.description:
Atomic Habits#

This serves as a reference to all the material covered as a part of the atomic habits seminar.

James Clear Articles#

Here is a link to some James Clear articles

Habits#

It is important for you to form the habits that will lead you to be the person you want to be. The discovery of this identity is first and foremost in your journey to adopt better and newer habits.

item.description: Atomic Habits Seminar#

item.title: Quizzes
item.description:
Quizzes#

The quizzes for each section of the seminar.

Quiz 1#

  1. Name the three layers of behavior change, from outermost to innermost. In which direction does lasting change occur?
  2. What should your primary focus be?
    • A) What you want to achieve
    • B) Who you wish to become
    • C) How quickly you can get there
    • D) What others expect of you
  3. “Identity First” implies ______________________________.
  4. “Cast Votes” implies ______________________________.
  5. “Language Shift” expects ______________________________.

Quiz 2#

  1. List the four stages of the Habit Loop, in order.
  2. Dopamine spikes at the _____ .
  3. Which type of reward spikes dopamine the hardest?
  4. “Just one more scroll” is hard to resist because the loop is built around a _____ .

Quiz 3#

  1. What do winners and losers have in common?
  2. A _____ is the direction and a _____ is the vehicle.
  3. Give four reasons why goal-only thinking is a problem.
  4. What problem do you see in each of the below examples for goal setting (as mentioned in the section)?
    • a. “Bill Gates dropped out of school to start Microsoft”
    • b. “I won the district level 100m sprint”
    • c. “I will be at peace once I get a Duke bike”
    • d. “I want to lose 8kgs of weight and today is the 4th day”

Quiz 4#

  1. Name the four laws of behavioural change.
  2. Which law does each of the following associate with?
    • a. Shrink the habit until starting takes no willpower
    • b. Design the cue so it’s impossible to miss
    • c. Make the win felt right away, every time
    • d. Pair the habit with something you already crave
  3. What are the three problems of relying on motivation?

Quiz 5#

  1. Give an example of how to apply Law 1 to build each of these habits:
    • A. Running
    • B. Keeping the fridge stocked with healthy food
    • C. Learning to play the guitar
    • D. Reading books
  2. Design the room ____________ .

Quiz 6#

  1. List the three groups of social influence.
  2. Name the influence group for each of the following:
    • a. We imitate people with status, hoping their behavior earns us the same respect
    • b. Family, partners, close friends shape what feels “normal” more than anyone else
    • c. A group pulls you toward its average without you noticing
  3. Give an example for temptation bundling.
  4. Give an example for habit stacking.
  5. Pair the hard thing with something _________ .

Quiz 7#

  1. Name the three tactics under “Make It Easy” covered in this section.
  2. The two-minute rule says: ________ .
  3. What’s the difference between “priming the environment” and “shrinking the habit”? Give one word or short phrase for each.
  4. The hardest part of any habit is ______ .
  5. Shrink it until _________ .
  6. Give the comparison between taking two minutes vs waiting for the mood once the cue appears.
  7. Phone lock-out after 10 pm is _____ tactic.
  8. Automate: a one time decision replaces _____ .

Quiz 8#

  1. Law 4 is about _____ .
  2. Name the three tactics this section teaches _____ .
  3. What gets rewarded ______ .
  4. How does marking an “X” on a calendar help?
  5. What’s an example of rewarding it immediately? Why does it work over reward it later?
  6. What is a tactic that results in your friend messaging whether you went for a run? Why is it important?
  7. Never let a good rep ____ .

Quiz 9#

  1. The section’s core rule: “Miss once _________ "
  2. What actually has the potential to kill a habit?
  3. If you skip a habit today, what happens tomorrow?
  4. The ice cube example is used to explain what about habits?
  5. What should you do during the flat stretch?
  6. What’s the difference between perfection and identity as the goal of a habit?
  7. One percent better daily = ___________ times.
  8. One percent worse daily = ___________ times.

Quiz 10#

  1. To break a bad habit ______ the four laws.
  2. Make the four laws relevant for this section and list them.
  3. Apply the laws to get off Instagram (give tactics).
  4. How to use “mark the calendar” to get off a bad habit?
  5. Why is a written witnessed contract better than a private promise to yourself?
  6. Give examples for the tactics of the four laws for this section.

item.title: Habit Challenge Cards
item.description:
Habit Challenge Cards#

Each card is a scenario. Your team designs the system that solves it, using the four laws — make it obvious, attractive, easy, and satisfying. For the cards under Breaking a Bad Habit, invert them: make it invisible, unattractive, hard, and unsatisfying.

Building a Good Habit#

Daily Reading Habit#

Your team is handed a fresh grad who reads zero pages a week. Design a system that gets them into a sustainable daily reading habit.

item.title: Getting Started
item.description: Welcome to STEP-12 Blog.

item.title: Particle Detector 2
item.description:
Extension — Scan in Two Directions#

Our particle detector has so far been scanning from left to right and back again.

That means we have been thinking about ranges along the horizontal direction.

But our region of space has two dimensions.

Why should we only scan horizontally?

A particle detector could also scan from top to bottom.

A New Direction#

Add another scanner to your simulation.

This scanner should move vertically.

item.title: Simple JS Practice
item.description:
JavaScript Practice#

Solve the following problems in JavaScript.

You have not learned traditional loops yet, so do not use for, while, or similar loops. Use recursion whenever you need to repeat an operation.

Write a separate function for each problem.

1. Simple Interest#

Write a function that calculates simple interest.

The function should take:

  • principal amount
  • rate of interest
  • time

and return the simple interest.

For example:

simpleInterest(1000, 5, 2) → 100

2. Compound Interest#

Write a function that calculates compound interest.

item.title: Particle Detector
item.description:
Scanning for Particles#

Imagine that we have sent a particle detector into space.

The detector is looking at a small region of space around it. It moves from one side of the region to the other, scanning for particles as it goes.

Our job is to build a simulation of this detector.

You will build the simulation in several steps. Each step adds one small idea to the previous one.

item.title: Template
item.description:
Modules and a Raylib Template#

So far, each Raylib program you have written has lived in a single file.

We have already started organizing that file into functions:

function setup() {}

function update() {}

function draw() {}

function loop() {
 while (!r.WindowShouldClose()) {
 update();
 draw();
 }
}

function main() {
 setup();
 loop();
}

main();

This gives different parts of the program different responsibilities.

But there is another kind of organization available to us.

We can separate our program into different files.

item.title: Intro to Git/GitHub
item.description:
So far, whatever the raylib code you wrote has stored on your computer.

Now think about these situations:

  • What if your laptop suddenly stops working?
  • What if you want your code reviewed by mentors or peers, may be during the weekend?
  • What if your laptop gets lost or damaged?
  • What if you want to access your code from another computer?
  • What if you are away from your laptop but need to look at your latest code?

All of these point to the same problem: your code lives in exactly one place.

item.title: Skeleton
item.description:
Organizing a Raylib Program#

You have now written a few small Raylib programs.

You have probably noticed that even a small program starts to contain several different kinds of code:

  • code that prepares the window
  • code that changes things
  • code that draws things
  • code that keeps the program running

It is useful to give these different responsibilities a little structure.

We are going to use the following skeleton:

function setup() {}

function update() {}

function draw() {}

function loop() {
 update();
 draw();
}

function main() {
 setup();
 loop();
}

main();

This is not a rule imposed by Raylib.

item.title: Simple exercises
item.description:
First Exercises#

You now have a working Raylib program.

You have seen how a Raylib program is structured, and you have used functions such as r.DrawRectangle.

Now it is time to start solving some small problems.

For these exercises, create a directory called:

workspace/raylib_exercises/

Each exercise should be its own program.

Use these filenames:

01_center_rectangle.js
02_center_rectangle_in_rectangle.js
03_scale_and_center.js
04_closer_target.js

Write the Raylib program yourself for each exercise. You should not need to copy the program from the previous post.

item.title: Raylib anatomy
item.description:
The anatomy of a Raylib program#

In the previous post, we saw that Raylib is a library that gives our JavaScript programs a collection of functions for working with graphics.

We are now going to look at a complete Raylib program.

Don’t worry if you don’t understand everything in it yet.

In fact, you shouldn’t.

Read through it once and see if you can recognize anything.

const r = require("raylib");

r.InitWindow(800, 400, "Raylib");
r.SetTargetFPS(60);

while (!r.WindowShouldClose()) {
 r.BeginDrawing();
 r.ClearBackground(r.BLACK);

 r.DrawRectangle(100, 50, 600, 300, r.WHITE);

 r.EndDrawing();
}

r.CloseWindow();

There are quite a few things happening here.

item.title: Intro to Graphics/Raylib
item.description:
Raylib#

So far, most of the programs you have written have produced things like numbers and text.

You might have written:

console.log(2 + 3);

and seen:

5

Or perhaps you wrote a function that takes some values, performs a computation, and returns another value.

What if the result of our program could be something that we could see?

What if instead of producing:

5

our program could produce a rectangle on the screen?

That is where we are going next.

item.title: JS Recursion
item.description:
Recursion Assignments#

For these assignments, you do not need to learn anything new about JavaScript. Use the things you already know: functions, parameters, return values, strings, numbers, conditionals, and basic operators.

There are three small problems.

1. Nested Parentheses#

Write a function that takes a number n and returns a string containing n pairs of nested parentheses.

For example:

5 → "((((()))))"

There are five opening parentheses followed by five closing parentheses.

item.title: More about functions
item.description:
Function calls inside function calls#

So far, you have seen function calls like this:

double(5)

When you see this, you know that double(5) is an expression. The function runs, and eventually the expression produces a value.

Let’s make the expression a little more interesting.

Suppose we have:

function double(number) {
 return number * 2;
}

function addOne(number) {
 return number + 1;
}

Now consider:

addOne(double(5))

Don’t run it yet.

What value should addOne receive?

Think about what has to happen first.

item.title: Functions
item.description:
You have now started writing JavaScript programs in files.

Until now, you have mostly been asking JavaScript questions in the REPL:

> 10 % 2 === 0
true

> 17 % 2 === 0
false

Now you can put those expressions into a program, save the program in a file, and run it.

Today, we are going to look at a problem that appears very quickly when you start writing larger programs:

item.title: Const, let, if etc
item.description:
From the REPL to the Editor#

So far, you have been programming in the REPL.

You have typed expressions such as:

5 + 3;

and:

10 > 5 && 20 < 30;

JavaScript evaluates them and the REPL shows you the result.

You have also spent time drawing expression trees.

You have learned to look at an expression, break it into smaller expressions, and follow the order in which those expressions are evaluated.

Now we are going to change something.

item.title: IDE (VSCode)
item.description:
IDE#

IDE stands for Integrated Development Environment.

An IDE is a development environment that brings together the tools needed to write, understand, run, and debug software. It provides a graphical interface that coordinates these tools and makes software development easier.

An IDE helps you:

  • Navigate code
  • Write and edit code
  • Run code
  • Debug code
  • Search and replace text
  • Manage files and folders
  • Integrate with version control
  • Install extensions for additional functionality

For this lesson, we will use VS Code as an example of an IDE.

item.title: In Defense of Light Mode
item.description:
I have reached an age at which I have become mildly irritated by the color scheme of my computer.

This is not, I should stress, an important problem.

There are wars, famines, elections, climate change, and JavaScript frameworks that have somehow acquired build systems larger than operating systems. And yet here I am, wanting to talk about light mode.

Because apparently I am now required to defend myself for wanting a white background behind my text.

item.title: The Kitchen
item.description:
The Kitchen#

Imagine that you are running a busy kitchen.

Not a small kitchen at home where one person makes breakfast.

A very busy kitchen.

There are many people who want to use it at the same time.

One person wants to make tea. Another wants to cook rice. Someone is baking bread. Someone else is making soup. Another person is washing dishes.

They all need things from the same kitchen:

item.title: Intro to JS part 2
item.description:
Strings can have properties#

Try:

"Hello".length;

You should get:

5

What do you think happened?

"Hello" is a string.

.length asks about something associated with that string.

Try:

"".length;
"Hello World".length;
"JavaScript".length;

Now try:

"Hello\nWorld";

What did you see?

The \n represents a newline.

You can experiment with other strings too.

Try making a string containing:

  • a quotation mark;
  • several lines;
  • a tab;
  • an empty string.

Don’t worry about remembering every escape sequence.

The REPL is available.

item.title: Intro to JS
item.description:
Your first language#

Until now, you’ve been talking to your computer through the shell.

You’ve typed commands. The shell has interpreted those commands, started processes, connected them together, and shown you their output.

Now we’re going to learn a programming language.

We’re going to start with JavaScript.

And we’re going to do something slightly different from what you might expect from a programming class.

For now, we’re not going to write a program.

item.title: JS Reference
item.description:
// ============================================================================
// JavaScript Language Reference
// ============================================================================
//
// A compact reference of JavaScript syntax and expressions.
// Every example in this file is valid JavaScript.
//
// ============================================================================



// ============================================================================
// COMMENTS
// ============================================================================

// This is a line comment.

/*
This is a
block comment.
*/



// ============================================================================
// LITERALS
// ============================================================================


// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Numbers
// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

0; // Zero is a valid number.
5; // A number evaluates to itself.
5.0; // Integers and decimals are both numbers.
5.25; // Numbers can have a fractional part.
-100.9999; // Numbers can be negative.
1e6; // Scientific notation for large numbers.
1e-3; // Scientific notation for small numbers.
0xff; // Hexadecimal literal (255).
0b1010; // Binary literal (10).
0o755; // Octal literal (493).
Infinity; // Positive infinity.
-Infinity; // Negative infinity.
NaN; // Represents "Not a Number".


// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Booleans
// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

true; // Boolean true.
false; // Boolean false.


// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Strings
// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

""; // The empty string.
"Hello"; // Double-quoted string.
'Hello'; // Single-quoted string.
`Hello`; // Template string using backticks.
"Hello\nWorld"; // Escape sequences insert special characters.


// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Other Primitive Values
// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

undefined; // Represents the absence of a value.
null; // Represents an intentional empty value.



// ============================================================================
// VARIABLES
// ============================================================================

let score = 0; // Declare a mutable variable.
let lives = 3; // Variables can be declared independently.

score = 100; // Variables can be reassigned.
score = score + 1; // Variables can use their current value.
lives = lives - 1; // Updating a variable is a common operation.

const width = 800; // Declare an immutable variable.
const height = 600; // Constants cannot be reassigned.



// ============================================================================
// ARITHMETIC OPERATORS
// ============================================================================


// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Binary Arithmetic
// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

5 + 3; // Addition.
5 - 3; // Subtraction.
5 * 3; // Multiplication.
5 / 2; // Division can produce decimals.
5 % 2; // Remainder after division.
2 ** 8; // Exponentiation (2 raised to the power of 8).


// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Unary Arithmetic
// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

let x = 5;

+x; // Unary plus converts a value to a number.
-x; // Unary minus negates a number.

++x; // Increment before the expression is evaluated.
x++; // Increment after the expression is evaluated.

--x; // Decrement before the expression is evaluated.
x--; // Decrement after the expression is evaluated.


// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
// Compound Assignment
// ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

let y = 10;

y += 5; // Equivalent to y = y + 5.
y -= 2; // Equivalent to y = y - 2.
y *= 3; // Equivalent to y = y * 3.
y /= 4; // Equivalent to y = y / 4.
y %= 2; // Equivalent to y = y % 2.
y **= 3; // Equivalent to y = y ** 3.


// ============================================================================
// COMPLEX ARITHMETIC EXPRESSIONS
// ============================================================================

2 + 3 * 5; // Multiplication happens before addition (17).

(2 + 3) * 5; // Parentheses change the order of evaluation (25).

10 - 2 * 3; // Multiplication happens before subtraction (4).

(10 - 2) * 3; // Parentheses force subtraction first (24).

20 / 2 + 5; // Division happens before addition (15).

20 / (2 + 3); // Parentheses change the divisor (4).

2 * 3 + 4 * 5; // Operators of the same precedence are evaluated left to right (26).

(2 * (3 + 4)) * 5; // Parentheses can be nested.

2 ** 3 * 4; // Exponentiation happens before multiplication (32).

2 * 3 ** 4; // Exponentiation has higher precedence than multiplication (162).

-(2 + 3); // Unary minus applies to the grouped expression (-5).

-2 ** 2; // Exponentiation happens before unary minus (-4).

(-2) ** 2; // Parentheses make the negative number the base (4).


// ============================================================================
// COMPARISON OPERATORS
// ============================================================================

5 == "5"; // Loose equality converts values before comparing.
5 != "6"; // Loose inequality also performs type coercion.

5 === 5; // Strict equality compares both type and value.
5 !== "5"; // Strict inequality compares both type and value.

5 < 10; // Less than.
5 > 2; // Greater than.
5 <= 5; // Less than or equal.
5 >= 5; // Greater than or equal.



// ============================================================================
// BOOLEAN OPERATORS
// ============================================================================

!true; // Logical NOT inverts a boolean.
true && false; // Logical AND requires both operands to be true.
true || false; // Logical OR requires at least one operand to be true.

5 > 3 && 10 < 20; // Boolean expressions can be combined with AND.
5 < 3 || 10 < 20; // OR succeeds if either expression is true.
!(5 === 5); // NOT negates the result of an expression.



// ============================================================================
// BITWISE OPERATORS
// ============================================================================

5 & 3; // Bitwise AND.
5 | 3; // Bitwise OR.
5 ^ 3; // Bitwise XOR.
~5; // Bitwise NOT.

5 << 1; // Shift bits left by one position.
5 >> 1; // Arithmetic right shift.
5 >>> 1; // Logical right shift.



// ============================================================================
// ASSIGNMENT OPERATORS
// ============================================================================

let value = 10;

value = 20; // Replace the current value.

value &&= 30; // Assign only if the current value is truthy.
value ||= 40; // Assign only if the current value is falsy.

let answer = null;

answer ??= 42; // Assign only if the value is null or undefined.



// ============================================================================
// TYPE OPERATOR
// ============================================================================

typeof 5; // Evaluates to "number".
typeof true; // Evaluates to "boolean".
typeof "Hello"; // Evaluates to "string".
typeof undefined; // Evaluates to "undefined".
typeof null; // Evaluates to "object" (historical JavaScript quirk).
typeof NaN; // NaN is still a number.



// ============================================================================
// TRUTHINESS
// ============================================================================

Boolean(true); // true remains true.
Boolean(false); // false remains false.

Boolean(1); // Non-zero numbers are truthy.
Boolean(0); // Zero is falsy.

Boolean("Hello"); // Non-empty strings are truthy.
Boolean(""); // The empty string is falsy.

Boolean(null); // null is falsy.
Boolean(undefined); // undefined is falsy.
Boolean(NaN); // NaN is falsy.



// ============================================================================
// CONDITIONAL EXPRESSIONS
// ============================================================================

true ? "yes" : "no"; // Chooses between two values.
5 > 3 ? 1 : 0; // The condition may be any boolean expression.



// ============================================================================
// STRING OPERATIONS
// ============================================================================

"Hello" + " World"; // Strings can be concatenated.
"Score: " + 10; // Non-strings are converted automatically.
`Score: ${10}`; // Template strings support interpolation.
"Hello\nWorld"; // Escape sequences create special characters.
"JavaScript".length; // Strings have useful properties.

item.title: Commands
item.description:
Commands#

We’ve seen that the shell reads what we type and either handles it itself or starts another process.

But what exactly are we typing?

ls -l ~/Downloads

This is a command.

Let’s take it apart.

The Anatomy of a Command#

A command generally starts with a command name.

ls

Here, ls is the name of the program we want to run.

We can provide additional information to the command using arguments and options.

item.title: Process, Terminals, Shells
item.description:
Process#

When your computer starts, the kernel is one of the first pieces of the operating system to start running. The kernel is responsible for managing the computer: its memory, CPU, devices, files and, importantly, the programs that are running.

But what does it mean for a program to be running?

From Program to Process#

A program starts life as a file on a storage device. When you install an application, its code is sitting on your disk or SSD.

item.title: More Recursion
item.description:
A Few More Loops to Avoid#

Liked the recursion problems?

Here are a few more.

Same rules as before: try to solve each problem by making the problem smaller, and let the function call itself.

Two Ways to Recur#

There are two common ways we will write recursive functions.

They do the same sort of work, but they keep track of things differently.

1. The Accumulator#

Sometimes we pass the answer-so-far as an argument.

item.title: More Functions in Math
item.description:
Functions — Beyond the Basics#

From mathematical functions to programming functions#

1. Where We Are#

We already know that a function:

  • Takes some input
  • Applies a rule
  • Produces an output
  • Has a domain and a range

For example:

f(x) = 2x + 3

If we give it 5:

f(5) = 2(5) + 3
 = 13

item.title: Functions in Math
item.description:
Functions — A Little Bit of Function#

1. What Is a Function?#

A function is a rule that takes an input and produces an output.

For example:

f(x) = 2x + 3

Give it 5:

f(5) = 2(5) + 3
 = 13

So we can think of a function as:

input → function → output

2. Evaluating Functions#

If:

f(x) = x² + 1

then:

f(2) = 2² + 1
 = 5

The x is simply replaced by the input.

item.title: Logic
item.description:
Logic: The Machinery of Reasoning#

You already know more logic than you think.

Every time you say:

“If it is raining, I should carry an umbrella.”

or:

“I will have tea if there is milk and sugar.”

or:

“I will go out if it is Saturday or Sunday.”

you are using logic.

You don’t need a computer, a formula, or a mathematics degree to use it. Logic is simply a way of describing how statements combine and how we reason from one statement to another.

item.description:
Ecnryption, Decryption, History…#

Puzzle#

Decrypt this puzzle. The clue is “12”. The other clue is “5”. It is important to consider both shapes and colors together.

Puzzle Image#

History#

  • Why this activity?
  • A brief history of computing
  • Entscheidungsproblem by David Hilbert
  • Kurt Gödel publishes his incompleteness theorems
  • Inspired by all this Alan Turing proves that a general solution to Hilbert’s question is impossible and proceeds to find a limit to what can be computed. In doing so he invents the Turing Machine which is what modern computers are primarily based on.
  • Turing gets enlisted by the British government to work in Bletchley Park on the Engima project
  • Germans use the Engima machine to encrypt messages and send to their troops. This proves very hard to crack
  • With some luck and ingenuity - and the clever use of a computer - Alan Turing solves this problem, thus setting off the modern computer age.
